Abstract 
Aim. Pulsed electromagnetic field (PEMF) therapy has been documented to be an effective, 
non-invasive, safe treatment method for a variety of clinical conditions, especially in settings 
of recalcitrant healing. The underlying mechanisms on the different biological components of 
tissue regeneration are still to be elucidated. The aim of the present study was to characterize 
the effects of extremely low frequency (ELF)-PEMFs on commitment of mesenchymal stem 
cell (MSCs) culture system, through the determination of gene expression pattern and cellular 
morphology. 
Main methods. Human MSCs derived from adipose tissue (ADSCs) were cultured in 
presence of adipogenic, osteogenic, neural, or glial differentiative medium and basal medium, 
then exposed to ELF-PEMFs daily stimulation for 21 days. Control cultures were performed 
without ELF-PEMFs stimulation for all cell populations. Effects on commitment were 
evaluated after 21 days of cultures. 
Key findings. The results suggested ELF-PEMFs does not influence ADSCs commitment and 
does not promote adipogenic, osteogenic, neural or glial differentiation. However, ELF-
PEMFs treatment on ADSCs cultured in osteogenic differentiative medium markedly 
increased osteogenesis. 
Significance. We concluded that PEMFs affect the osteogenic differentiation of ADSCs only 
if they are pre-commitment and that this therapy can be an appropriate candidate for 
treatment of conditions requiring an acceleration of repairing process. 
 
 
Key words: adipose-derived stem cells; pulsed electromagnetic fields; osteogenic 
commitment; bone regeneration.

Introduction 
Pulsed electromagnetic field (PEMF) therapy is successfully in use in modern medicine [1]. It 
is based on the physical effect sorted from the combination of an electric with a magnetic 
field, generating waves that propagate at the speed of light [2]. Human clinical trials and 
animal experiments have shown that electromagnetic stimulation accelerates wound healing 
and bone formation, carrying the promise of a safe, non-invasive treatment for challenging 
conditions such as non-healing ulcers, bone mal-union, and chronic inflammatory diseases 
[3-7]. Extremely low frequency (ELF)-PEMF instruments, like Therapeutic Magnetic 
Resonance (TMR®) device, generate shorts bursts of electrical current which have been 
demonstrated to increase cell proliferation and extracellular matrix (ECM) component 
synthesis [8-12]. This enhances the tissue regenerative potential and wound healing response, 
as growth factor signaling is influenced by low frequency electromagnetic signals. 
Although the positive effects exerted by PEMFs are well documented, the reasons for the 
reactions of the biological systems still remain unidentified. The biological response could be 
driven by a stem cell-mediated action, with mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) possibly playing 
the greatest role. MSCs are hosted in specific microenvironments referred to as “niches”, 
which constitute basic physical units where cell-cell and tissue-cell signals are integrated, 
ultimately determining stem cells response [13,14]. Some theories hypothesize the induction 
of a mechanical response of MSCs to electromagnetic fields, which would induce stem cells 
to emerge from the niches promoting tissue regeneration [15]. Other studies have described a 
possible effect on stem cells commitment, with electromagnetic therapy modulating MSCs 
ability to “switch” among different phenotypes forming cartilage, fat, myogenic, and neural-
like tissue [13-18]. However, the effect of PEMFs on stem cells as key players in tissue 
regeneration remains to be investigated.

This study focuses on the effects of ELF-PEMFs on commitment of a ubiquitous MSCs 
subpopulation, adipose-derived stem cells (ADSCs), in an in vitro model. The results may 
contribute to enhancing the knowledge in the field of pulsed magnetic therapy and may 
support further stem cell-therapeutics and clinical application. 
 
Materials and Methods 
Isolation of ADSCs 
Adipose tissue samples were obtained from the abdominal region of six healthy patients 
(aged 35-58) undergoing abdominoplasty, after acquiring written consent, according to the 
Guidelines provided by the Clinic of Plastic Surgery of Padua University Hospital. The 
samples were washed in phosphate-buffered saline (PBS, EuroClone, Milan, Italy) and cut 
into 1 cm2 pieces. The tissue was digested with a solution of 0.075% collagenase from 
Clostridium hystolyticum Type II (Sigma-Aldrich, St. Louis, MO, USA) in Hank's Balanced 
Salts Solution (HBSS, Lonza, Milano, Italy) and placed under stirring for 3 hours at room 
temperature. After digestion was completed, collagenase activity was quenched with an equal 
volume of basal medium composed of Dulbecco’s modified Eagle’s medium (DMEM, 
Lonza), 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS, EuroClone) and 1% Penicillin/Streptomycin (P/S, 
Lonza). Indigested material was removed by filtration, and eluate was centrifuged at 1200 
rpm for 4 minutes. Cells were seeded in basal medium into 75 cm2 tissue culture flask, and 
incubated at 5% CO2 and 37° C. Culture medium was changed every 2 days. 
 
Adipogenic and osteogenic differentiation of ADSCs 
ADSCs, amplified up to passage 2, were harvested by trypsin treatment (trypsin/EDTA, 
EuroClone). Cells were counted under Bürker Chamber (Paul Marienfeld GmbH & Co. KG, 
Lauda-Königshofen, Germany), then seeded at a density of 15 x 103 cells/cm2 in 24-well

ACCEPTED MANUSCRIPT
ACCEPTED MANUSCRIPT
 
5 
 
plates. The cultures were incubated in adipogenic or osteogenic differentiation medium up to 
21 days. Adipogenic differentiation medium was made of DMEM high glucose (Lonza) 
supplemented with 10% FBS, 1% P/S, 10 µg/mL insulin (Sigma-Aldrich), 0.5 mM 
isobutylmethylxanthine (IBMX, Sigma-Aldrich), 0.1 mM indomethacin (Sigma-Aldrich), and 
1 µM dexamethasone (Sigma-Aldrich). Osteogenic differentiation medium was composed of 
DMEM high glucose supplemented with 10% FBS, 1% P/S, 10 ng/mL Fibroblast Growth 
Factor 2 (FGF-2, ProSpec, East Brunswick, NJ, USA), 10 mM β-glycerophosphate (Sigma-
Aldrich), and 10 nM dexamethasone. Experiments were performed with three different cell 
preparations and repeated three times. 
 
Neuronal and glial differentiation of ADSCs 
Cells obtained from the digestion of adipose tissue were seeded at a density of 105 cells/cm2, 
and cultured in proliferation medium at 5% CO2 and 37° C for 14 days. Proliferation medium 
consisted of DMEM-HAM’s F12 (3:1, EuroClone), 10% FBS, 1% P/S, 20 ng/mL Epidermal 
Growth Factor (EGF, ProSpec), and 40 ng/mL FGF-2. In order to induce neuronal and glial 
differentiation, cells were then seeded at a density of 15 x 103 cells/cm2 onto poly-D-lysine 
24-well plates and cultured for 21 days alternatively with neuronal or glial differentiation 
medium. The neuronal differentiation medium consisted of NeuroBasal Medium (Gibco by 
Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA) containing 1% FBS, 1% P/S, 2% b27 serum-
free supplement (Gibco), 10 μg/mL human recombinant beta nerve growth factor (bNGF, 
ProSpec), 100 ng/mL human recombinant brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF, 
ProSpec), and 20 ng/mL human recombinant neurotrophin-3 (NT3, ProSpec). Glial 
differentiation medium was made of NeuroBasal Medium containing 1% FBS, 1% P/S, 1% 
N2 supplement (Gibco), 4 μM forskolin (Merck Millipore, Darmstadt, Germany), and 10

ng/mL human recombinant heregulin-β (ProSpec). Experiments were performed with three 
different cell preparations and repeated three times. 
 
TMR® treatment 
Cell cultures were exposed to ELF-PEMFs from DIAPASON® device (Thereson S.p.A, 
Vimercate, MB, Italy). As previously described [8], the DIAPASON® device is composed of 
a console that generates electrical signals and an emitter connected to the console that 
converts the electrical signals into PEMFs. The emitter comprises two solenoids with 36 turns 
of copper wire of 0.8 mm diameter. The signal comprises a plurality of base pulses grouped 
in pulse packets and in pulse trains, in which each pulse packet consists of a series of base 
pulses followed by a first pause, in which each pulse train consists of a series of pulse packets 
followed by a second pause. The control circuit is configured to reverse the polarity of the 
base pulses after a given time interval. The frequency of the base pulses is 100 Hz, and the 
repetition frequency of the pulse packet is 2.89-25.9 Hz. The repetition frequency of pulse 
trains is 0.3-2.8 Hz, while the time interval is 120-180 seconds. The repetition frequency of 
the train sets is 0.1-0.3 Hz. The average amplitude of the generated magnetic field is less than 
40 μTesla (comparable to the Earth’s magnetic field). The treatment consisted of a daily 
stimulation of the cell cultures up to 21 days. In detail, cells cultured in 24-well plates were 
positioned in correspondence of the two solenoids of the DIAPASON® device, then exposed 
to ELF-PEMFs for 24 minutes at room temperature. Control cultures were performed 
positioned on the device in the same manner as the exposed cultures but without receiving 
ELF-PEMFs stimulation. 
 
Real time PCR

ACCEPTED MANUSCRIPT
 
7 
 
Total RNA was isolated from each cell culture by using the RNeasy Mini Kit (Qiagen GmbH, 
Hilden, Germany), including DNase digestion with the RNase-Free DNase Set (Qiagen). For 
the first-strand cDNA synthesis, 500 ng of total RNA of each sample was reverse transcribed 
with M-MLV Reverse Transcriptase (Invitrogen, Carlsbad, CA, USA), following the 
manufacturer’s protocol. Human primers were selected for each target gene with Primer 3 
software. Real-time PCRs were carried out using the designed primers at a concentration of 
300 nM and FastStart SYBR Green Master (Roche Diagnostics, Mannheim, Germany) on a 
Rotor-Gene 3000 (Corbett Research, Sydney, Australia). Thermal cycling conditions were as 
follows: 15 minutes denaturation at 95°C; followed by 40 cycles of denaturation for 15 
seconds at 95°C; annealing for 30 seconds at 60°C; and elongation for 20 seconds at 72°C. 
Cell cultures that were not subjected to ELF-PEMFs stimulation were used as control 
condition. Values were normalized to the expression of the transferrin receptor (TFRC) 
internal reference, whose abundance did not change under our experimental conditions. 
 
Lipid content 
Oil Red O quantification was used to evaluate the intracellular lipid content. Oil Red O stock 
solution was prepared by dissolving 3.5 mg/mL Oil Red O (Sigma-Aldrich) in isopropanol. 
Working solution consisted of 3:2 Oil Red O stock in ddH2O. Cell cultures were incubated in 
0.5 mL of Oil Red O working solution for 15 minutes at room temperature. After washing in 
ddH2O, Oil Red O was extracted with 0.25 mL 100% isopropanol. For each sample, optical 
density (O.D.) values at 490 nm were recorded using a multilabel plate reader (Victor 3 
Perkin Elmer, Milano, Italy). 
 
Alkaline phosphatase assay 

--- Page 9 ---

ACCEPTED MANUSCRIPT
ACCEPTED MANUSCRIPT
 
8 
 
The intracellular Alkaline phosphatase (ALP) activity was detected with a colorimetric 
Alkaline Phosphatase Assay Kit (Abcam, Cambridge, UK). Cells were washed with PBS, 
homogenized with ALP Assay Buffer, then centrifuged at 13 000 rpm for 3 minutes to 
remove insoluble material. A standard curve was drawn using the corrected absorbance 
values of standards, and the pNP concentration was identified for each sample. ALP activity 
was calculated as follows: ALP activity (U/mL) = (A/V)/T, where A represents the amount of 
pNP generated by samples (in μmol), V is the volume of sample added in the assay well (in 
mL), and T is the reaction time (in minutes). 
 
Alizarin Red S staining 
The extracellular mineral deposits were detected by Alizarin Red S staining. Cells were fixed 
in 4% paraformaldehyde (Sigma-Aldrich) in PBS for 10 minutes at room temperature. Cells 
were stained adding 40 mM freshly Alizarin Red S Solution (pH 4.2) for 10 minutes at room 
temperature with gentle shaking. Cells were washed with ddH2O, then photographed by an 
optical microscope. Alizarin Red S stained area were quantified from microscope images of 
three independent experiments using Image J software (NIH, Bethesda, MD, USA). 
 
Von Kossa staining 
Cells were fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde in PBS for 10 minutes at room temperature, then 
incubated with 5% silver nitrate solution under ultraviolet light for 1 hour. After washing 
with ddH2O, unreacted silver was removed with 5% sodium thiosulfate for 5 minutes. Cells 
were washed with ddH2O, counterstained with nuclear fast red for 5 minutes, then washed 
again in ddH2O. Cells were observed under an optical microscope. 
 
Immunofluorescence

ACCEPTED MANUSCRIPT
ACCEPTED MANUSCRIPT
 
9 
 
Cells were fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde in PBS for 10 minutes, then incubated in 2% 
bovine serum albumin (BSA, Sigma-Aldrich) in PBS for 30 minutes at room temperature. 
Cells were then incubated with primary antibodies in 2% BSA solution in a humidified 
chamber for 12 hours at 4° C. The following primary antibodies were used: rabbit polyclonal 
anti-human osteocalcin antibody (Millipore Corporation, MA, USA), and mouse polyclonal 
anti-human collagen type I antibody (Sigma-Aldrich). Immunofluorescence staining was 
performed using the secondary antibodies DyLight 549-labeled anti-rabbit IgG (H+L) (KPL, 
Gaithersburg, MD, USA), and DyLight 488-labeled anti-mouse IgG (KPL) diluted 1∶1000 in 
2% BSA for 1 hour at room temperature. Nuclear staining was performed with 2 µg/mL 
Hoechst H33342 (Sigma-Aldrich) solution for 2 minutes. 
 
Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) 
For SEM imaging, cells were fixed in 2.5% glutaraldehyde in 0.1 M cacodylate buffer for 1 
hour, then progressively dehydrated in ethanol. All micrographs were obtained at 30 kV on a 
JEOL 6360LV SEM microscope (JEOL, Tokyo, Japan). The SEM analysis was carried out at 
the Interdepartmental Service Center C.U.G.A.S. (University of Padua, Italy). 
 
Statistical analysis 
One-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) was used for data analyses. Repeated-measures 
ANOVA with post-hoc analysis using Bonferroni’s multiple comparison was performed. T 
test was used to determine significant differences (p≤0.05). Repeatability was calculated as 
the standard deviation of the difference between measurements. All testing was performed in 
SPSS 16.0 software (SPSS Inc., Chicago, IL, USA). 
 
Results

Preparation of human ADSCs cultures 
In order to investigate how ELF-PEMFs influence stem cells in tissue repair processes, we 
have prepared in vitro different human ADSCs cultures. In particular, we have cultured 
ADSCs in basal medium, and in osteogenic, adipogenic, neuronal or glial differentiation 
medium for 21 days. Cell populations were exposed to ELF-PEMFs all through the culture 
process. Non-exposed populations were used as control condition. 
Effects of ELF-PEMFs on undifferentiated ADSCs 
A gene expression profile analysis for osteogenic, adipogenic, neuronal, and glial markers 
was performed on ADSCs after 21 days of culture in basal medium. As shown in Figure 1A, 
there were no differences in mRNA expression of these markers between ELF-PEMFs-
exposed cell population and control. The expression of some angiogenic markers in the 
ADSCs cultures grown in basal medium has been additionally evaluated. Significant increase 
in expression level of mRNA related to angiogenesis was detected in cultures exposed to 
ELF-PEMFs in comparison to control (Fig. 1B). In particular, hypoxia inducible factor 
(HIF1A), and vascular endothelial growth factor A (VEGFA), VEGFB, and VEGFC resulted 
over-expressed in the exposed ADSCs with respect to the non-exposed ones. Also, mRNAs 
expression level of cell division cycle 42 (CDC42), and ras homolog family (RHO) were 
higher for cells exposed to PEMFs. These findings may suggest an effect of ELF-PEMFs on 
mechano-transduction processes, such as cell polarization, cell-to-cell interaction, and cell 
migration.

PEMFs exposure compared to non-exposed ADSCs. A. Gene expression level of adipogenic, 
neuronal, glial, and osteogenic markers. B. Gene expression level of angiogenic and

Effects of ELF-PEMFs on adipogenic-committed ADSCs 
The adipogenic commitment of ADSCs was confirmed by the detection of lipid droplets in 
the cytoplasm of the cells. These droplets were visible for both ELF-PEMFs-exposed cells 
and non-exposed cells after 21 days of culture in adipogenic differentiation medium (Fig. 2A 
and B, respectively). Oil Red O quantification showed no significant differences between the 
two cell populations for intracellular lipid content (Fig. 2C). Also gene expression analysis of 
adipogenic differentiation markers, such as proliferator-activated receptor gamma (PPARG), 
CCAAT/enhancer-binding proteins alpha (C/EBPA), and solute carrier family 2 (facilitated 
glucose transporter) member 4 (GLUT4) showed no significant difference (Fig. 2D).

magnification) of ADSCs exposed to ELF-PEMFs. B. Phase-contrast image (10X

Effects of ELF-PEMFs on neuronal- and glial-committed ADSCs 
The neuronal and glial differentiation of ADSCs was evaluated through gene expression 
analysis after 21 days of culture in neuronal and glial differentiation media. Regarding the 
neuronal commitment, the following markers were considered: growth associated protein 43 
(GAP43), encoding for a protein which is expressed at high levels in neural cones during 
axonal development and regeneration; microtubule associated protein 2 (MAP2), encoding 
for a protein belonging to the microtubule-associated protein family; and neurofilament light 
polypeptide (NEFL), belonging to the family of neurofilaments comprising the axoskeleton. 
For glial differentiation, we evaluated the expression of cadherin 19 type 2 (CDH19), 
expressed in glial cell precursors; glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP), an intermediate 
filament protein expressed in central nervous system and astrocytes; S100 calcium binding

the genes considered, no significant differences were detected between ELF-PEMFs-exposed 
cell population and control (Fig. 3). 
 
 
Figure 3. Analysis of expression of genes involved in neuronal and glial commitment. 
ADSCs exposed to 21-days ELF-PEMFs are compared to non-exposed ADSCs. Data 
presented as mean ± standard error (3 measurements). * p=0.05; ** p=0.01; *** p=0.001. 
 
Effects of ELF-PEMFs on osteogenic-committed ADSCs 
The osteogenic commitment of ADSCs was first evaluated by detection of extracellular 
calcium deposition through Alizarin Red S and Von Kossa stainings at 21 culture days (Fig. 
4). A visual difference for presence of calcium depots and osteoids could be assessed 
between pre-committed ADSCs receiving ELF-PEMFs (Fig. 4A and D) and controls (Fig. 4B 
and E), staining higher in the first population. The promotion of osteogenic differentiation of 
pre-committed ADSCs was also confirmed by quantification of Alizarin Red S stained area. 
A greater accumulation of calcium depots was indeed measured in ADSCs exposed to ELF-
PEMFs compared to the control cultures (Fig. 4C).

As for analysis of gene expression for osteogenic differentiation, the following markers were 
considered: osteocalcin (OC), which is secreted solely by osteoblasts and is pro-osteoblastic 
by nature, with implications in bone mineralization and calcium homeostasis [19]; 
osteonectin (ON), a calcium-binding glycoprotein secreted by osteoblasts during bone 
formation, initiating mineralization and promoting mineral crystal formation [20]; 
osteopontin (OPN), which is involved in osteoclasts attachment to the mineralized bone 
matrix [21]; alkaline phosphatase tissue non-specific isoenzyme (ALP), a membrane-bound 
glycosylated enzyme with the assumed function of promoting matrix mineralization [22]; 
collagen type I alpha 1 (COL1A1), a fibril-forming collagen found in most connective tissues

when compared to controls at 21 culture days. To further evaluate the effect of treatment of 
osteogenic commitment, intracellular ALP activity (expressed as U/mL) was quantified after 
7 and 21 days (Fig. 5B).

Cells exposed to PEMFs showed a significantly higher ALP activity level after 21 days when 
compared to control. Morphological analyses were also performed in order to evaluate the 
presence of specific osteogenic markers, as OC and COL1A1. As shown in Figure 6, staining 
was positive for all cell populations, but with a visually greater result for ADSCs exposed to

cells (750X magnification). 
 
Discussion 
ELF-PEMFs therapy is currently in use for skin ulcers, surgical recalcitrant wounds, and 
neuropathic pain [25,26]. Particularly, the clinical applications of PEMFs have been 

--- Page 18 ---

ACCEPTED MANUSCRIPT
ACCEPTED MANUSCRIPT
 
17 
 
concentrated on the treatment of the complications of diabetes mellitus. In 2015, Abruzzese 
et al. [27] demonstrated a positive effect of low-intensity TMR in the surgical management of 
empyema in the diabetic foot: a consecutive application of 14 days after surgical debridement 
was associated with a decrease in healing time, a higher rate of granulation tissue, and an 
increase in healing rate at 6 months, compared to standard treatment. Further in vitro study by 
Ferroni et al. [8] investigated the effects of PEMFs on skin wound healing. Tests on tissue 
from both healthy and diabetic donors showed an acceleration of fibroblasts and endothelial 
cells growth after exposure to TMR. Results were confirmed by Kwan et al. [4], reporting 
how PEMFs treatment stimulates early production of collagen and development of a vascular 
network, enhancing the repair of damaged tissue. Moreover, cell aging seems to be slowed by 
PEMFs, as a reduction of ROS production was observed [8]. However, chronic complicated 
wounds are still a biomedical burden, and new therapies are advocated to optimize the 
outcome for diabetic patients [28]. 
Stem cells, with their unique properties to self-renew and undergo differentiation, are the 
most promising candidate for novel therapeutics in the field of regenerative medicine  [29]. 
They can enhance wound healing by releasing inflammatory mediators, key cytokines, and 
growth factors, alongside with directly partaking to the wound healing process by 
commitment and differentiation [30]. In this view, we investigated the effects of TMR 
treatment on ADSCs in order to deepen the knowledge on how ELF-PEMFs influence stem 
cells in tissue repair processes. Human ADSCs were cultured in non-inductive or inductive 
differentiation medium for 21 days. Cell populations were exposed to ELF-PEMFs all 
through the culture process, with non-exposed populations used as a control. Our findings 
showed ELF-PEMFs had no effect on differentiation of non-committed ADSCs, which 
maintained their multipotency. However, TMR could increase regenerative processes through 
an improvement of vascularization, as suggested by the increase detection of HIF and VEGF 

--- Page 19 ---

ACCEPTED MANUSCRIPT
ACCEPTED MANUSCRIPT
 
18 
 
expression. Results also put in evidence a positive influence on cell activation and 
polarization: increased expression of RHO suggests a marked effect on mechano-
transduction, cell-cell interaction, and cell migration [31]. Following RHO expression, a 
sustained activation of CDC42 is usually observed, as was in our study, and it is usually 
associated with process as de novo formation of adherens junction  [32]. CDC42 has a 
primary role in establishing cell polarity and apical-basal axis in epithelial cells and in 
differentiating neurons, interacting with proteins that regulate endocytosis. It also controls 
epithelial tissue morphogenesis by regulating spindle orientation during cell division [33]. 
Within stem cells population, CDC42 has been strongly related to their ability to migrate 
[34]. 
As for pre-committed ADSCs, we found TMR treatment did not have relevant effects on 
adipogenic commitment. Expression of adipocyte differentiation markers, like C/EBPA, 
PPARG and GLUT4, were similar for cells exposed to ELF-PEMFs and non-exposed cells. 
The number of adipocytes present in an organism is determined to a large degree by the 
adipocyte differentiation process, which generates mature adipocytes from fibroblast-like pre-
adipocytes. In the differentiation process, the C/EBPA and PPARG act as key determinants in 
terminal adipocyte differentiation [35]. The finding that PEMFs does not enhance adipogenic 
differentiation could be interpreted positively, as an increase in adipocytes number or size 
would increase adipose tissue mass, contributing to insulin resistance and worsening pre-
existing diabetes [36]. 
Neurogenic commitment of ADSCs was also not influenced by TMR application. For both 
neuronal and glial induction, the markers expression levels did not show any significant 
difference. This result could be in contrast with evidences in literature describing the positive 
effect of PEMFs in the treatment of diabetic neuropathy, a disabling complication of diabetes 
caused by axonal degeneration in nerve fibers and primary demyelination from Schwann cell

dysfunction [37-40]. However, it is likely that the positive effects of PEMFs rely more on an 
enhanced neoangiogenesis in peripheral nerves than on an increased cell differentiation rate 
into neuronal or glial cells. 
Ultimately, we observed as for ADSCs cultured in osteogenic medium, the exposure to 
PEMFs strongly enhanced the commitment into mature osteoblasts, as revealed by gene 
expression, ALP activity, and morphological evaluations. Therefore we suggest TMR could 
potentially be beneficial to patients suffering from bone-related diseases, such as non-union 
fractures. Non-union fracture is a pathological condition having some impairment of the 
cellular part of bone repair: a decrease population of MSCs and of the osteoblastic activation. 
Non-union is therefore a good indication for cell-based therapies using stem cells. In effect, 
several clinical studies have demonstrated that MSCs transplantation could improve bone 
healing in non-unions [41,42]. In this view, the enhanced osteogenic differentiation that we 
have observed after exposing pre-committed ADSCs to PEMFs suggests that this therapy 
could be an appropriate candidate for treatment of such conditions requiring an acceleration 
of the repairing process. 
 
Conclusions 
Our results showed that TMR promotes the osteogenic differentiation of ADSCs if they are 
pre-committed by osteogenic medium. On the other hand, it showed no influence on 
adipogenic, neuronal, or glial commitment. In the absence of differential media, TMR® did 
not influence differentiation or lineage-specific gene expression. Nonetheless, a positive 
effect on neoangiogenesis and cell mobilization could be observed. These findings suggest 
TMR® as a useful treatment method for clinical conditions requiring an enhancement of bone 
reparative and regeneration processes, making it safe for application on diabetic patients as 
no increase in adiposity was demonstrated. The promotion of osteogenic differentiation could

More detailed studies are needed to understand the relationship between biological effects
